passage:
Monday: Joseph was stacking blocks into a tall tower when Joseph's mama, Aparna, called from the kitchen, "Shoes on, please!" Joseph kept stacking. The bus was missed.
Tuesday: Aparna walked over, crouched to eye level, and said, "Joseph." Joseph looked up. "Shoes on, please." Joseph fetched them right away.
Wednesday: Joseph was rolling a toy train along the sofa. Aparna crouched beside it and said, "Joseph." The train stopped. "Shoes?" said Joseph, and ran to the door.

qa.q: What was Joseph doing on Monday when Aparna called from the kitchen?
qa.a: Stacking blocks into a tall tower.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when Aparna called from the kitchen?
qa.a: Deeply interested in the tower of blocks, so Joseph heard the sound but did not take in the words.

qa.q: What change did Aparna make on Tuesday that helped?
qa.a: Aparna walked over, crouched to eye level and said Joseph's name first, then gave the instruction.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt on Monday when the bus was missed?
qa.a: Frustrated and hurried, perhaps thinking Joseph was ignoring the call, when Joseph had not really taken it in.

grounding: A child hears Mama's instruction while absorbed in play and does not process it; eye level and a name call help.

passage: The railway platform was loud with announcements and rolling suitcases. Chetan stood watching pigeons peck at crumbs near the yellow line, right in front of a waiting bag trolley. Chetan's mum, Simran, called out, "Chetan, hold my hand!" once, then again. Chetan did not turn; the pigeons were the whole world. A train horn sounded in the distance. Simran stepped over, crouched, touched Chetan's shoulder and said, "Chetan." Chetan's eyes came round. "Look at me. Hold my hand, the train is coming." Chetan's small hand slipped into Simran's, and they moved back from the yellow line together.

qa.q: What was Chetan watching on the platform?
qa.a: Pigeons pecking at crumbs near the yellow line.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when Simran called out?
qa.a: Completely caught up in curiosity about the pigeons, so Chetan heard the noise but the words did not sink in.

qa.q: What did Simran change that finally worked?
qa.a: Simran stepped over, crouched, touched Chetan's shoulder and said the name, then gave a short instruction once Chetan looked.

qa.q: How might Simran have felt when the train horn sounded and Chetan did not turn?
qa.a: Worried and hurried, since the noise was loud, Chetan was near the yellow line, and calling from a distance was not working.

grounding: A child hears Mum's instruction while looking at something else and does not process it; eye level and a name call help, even in a noisy place.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house near Hubli, Mehak, five, was playing with the new kittens. Her big brother Karthik called from the doorway, "Mehak, wash your hands, lunch is ready!" Mehak kept stroking the kittens. "Mehak! Lunch!" Nothing. Karthik walked over, crouched down beside her, and said, "Mehak," and waited until she looked at him. Then, softly: "Wash your hands now. Lunch." Mehak blinked. "Oh! Okay!" She put down the kitten and ran to the tap.

qa.q: What was Mehak playing with?
qa.a: The new kittens.

qa.q: Why didn't Mehak respond the first two times?
qa.a: She was so absorbed and happy with the kittens that she heard the voice but didn't take in the words.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that worked?
qa.a: He crouched to her level, said her name, waited until she looked at him, and then spoke.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt after calling twice?
qa.a: He was probably a little frustrated at first, but found a calm way to get her attention.

grounding: Shows a young child who hears an instruction while absorbed in play and doesn't process it, until an adult gets to eye level and uses her name first.

passage: In their London flat, Elif, four, was building a tall tower of blocks. Her father, Emeka, called from the kitchen, "Elif, put your shoes on, we're going to the park." Elif added another block. "Elif, shoes!" She didn't look up. Emeka came over and knelt beside her. "Elif." She looked at him. "Shoes on, then the park." Elif's eyes went wide. "The park? Yay!" She left the tower and ran for her shoes.

qa.q: What was Elif building?
qa.a: A tall tower of blocks.

qa.q: What does Elif's wide-eyed 'The park? Yay!' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was excited and hadn't really heard about the park before, because her attention was on the tower.

qa.q: What worked better than calling from the kitchen?
qa.a: Kneeling beside her and saying her name first, so she looked at him before he gave the instruction.

qa.q: How might Emeka feel when Elif finally hears him?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and amused that she was so happy once she actually heard the plan.

grounding: Shows a child who hears a parent's instruction while focused on a toy but doesn't process it, until the parent gets to her level and uses her name.

passage: At the preschool in Ahmedabad, Shankar sir said to the class, "Everyone, put your crayons in the box and come to the mat." Most children moved. Aparna, five, kept colouring her elephant, lost in it. Shankar sir said it again. Nothing. He walked over, knelt down beside her, and said, "Aparna." She looked up. "Crayons in the box, then the mat." Aparna looked at the empty tables in surprise. "Oh!" She dropped her crayons in the box and hurried over.

qa.q: What was Aparna colouring?
qa.a: An elephant.

qa.q: How did Aparna seem to feel when she noticed the empty tables?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and a little startled, not having noticed the class moving.

qa.q: What small step helped Aparna follow the instruction?
qa.a: Shankar sir knelt beside her and said her name first, getting her attention before repeating the instruction.

qa.q: How might the other children see Aparna staying at the table?
qa.a: They may not notice much, or they may think she was just busy colouring.

grounding: Shows a child who hears an instruction while absorbed in her colouring and does not process it, until a teacher kneels and says her name.

passage:
Monday. "Lakshmi, put your shoes on, we're leaving," Mama called from the kitchen. Lakshmi, building a block tower, said "Okay," and kept building. Five minutes later, still no shoes. Baljeet sighed loudly.
Wednesday. Baljeet tried something new. She walked over, knelt down to Lakshmi's height and waited until Lakshmi looked up. "Lakshmi. Shoes on, then tower later." Lakshmi blinked, nodded, and went.
Friday. Baljeet only had to kneel and say "Lakshmi" before Lakshmi put the block down herself and looked up, waiting for the words.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi building on Monday?
qa.a: She was building a block tower.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say "Okay" but not put her shoes on?
qa.a: She was absorbed and happy in her tower, so she heard the words without really taking them in, not because she was being defiant.

qa.q: What small change helped Lakshmi listen?
qa.a: Kneeling to her height, saying her name and waiting for her eyes before giving one short instruction.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel on Monday compared with Friday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt frustrated enough to sigh loudly; by Friday she was probably relieved that Lakshmi looked up after just her name.

grounding: Shows a young child who hears an instruction while absorbed in play without taking it in, and a parent getting her attention first.
